title: Influence of context and setting on the mental health and wellbeing outcomes of ayahuasca drinkers: Results of a large international survey

claims.statement: In an international online survey of people who had drunk ayahuasca (2017 to 2019; 6,877 self-selected respondents who had drunk with no more than two groups; Perkins et al., 2021), the setting of their last ceremony, as they described and rated it looking back, was associated with how much extreme fear they recalled and with difficulties afterwards, by small amounts. Of the 6,817 with a known setting, 52.1% had last drunk in an ayahuasca church (87% of them living in Brazil, and more than half having drunk over 200 times), 19.6% with traditional shamans and 28.3% in other settings, where most had drunk five times or fewer. Adjusted for age, sex, education, number of mental-health diagnoses, times drunk, years since the last drink and the other setting variables, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety (averages 3.4 to 3.9) went with less extreme fear or panic (−0.29 on a 0-to-10 scale, SE 0.07) and fewer difficulties in the weeks after (−0.13, SE 0.05); each point higher on a rating of the preparation offered (a chance to discuss one's history and concerns, and guidance on difficulties, before drinking) went with fewer later difficulties (−0.14, SE 0.03) but not with less fear (−0.01, p = 0.82). More fear went with more traditional practices (0.18 per practice, of up to 6), with drinking mostly in Amazonian countries other than Brazil (0.7), with therapeutic reasons for drinking (0.21 per reason) and with mental-health diagnoses (0.21 per diagnosis); less fear went with church features such as hymns or sermons (−0.38) and with each decade of age (−0.22). Fasting, offered at 35% of traditional and 26% of other settings, was associated with no difference in fear, later difficulties or current mental health, and with slightly higher ratings of mystical experience (1.7 points on a 9-to-90 scale) and of growth in well-being. Across the whole range of either rating, current distress differed by under 2 points on the 40-point Kessler scale (editors' arithmetic). Ratings and outcomes were reported by the same people at one sitting, on average 1.2 to 1.6 years after their last drink; nothing was measured before ayahuasca, the amount and content of the brew were not recorded, and the authors note that the sample may lean towards people with good experiences. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Adjusted B (SE): support and safety (per point, 1 to 4) extreme fear −0.29 (0.07), later difficulties −0.13 (0.05), Kessler-10 −0.62 (0.12); preparation offered (per point) later difficulties −0.14 (0.03), fear −0.01 (p = 0.82), Kessler-10 −0.25 (0.07); extreme fear: traditional practices 0.18 per practice, traditional country 0.7, therapeutic motivation 0.21, mental-health diagnoses 0.21, church features −0.38, age −0.22 per decade; fasting: no association with fear, later difficulties or mental health, mystical orientation 1.69 (0.64), growth 0.97 (0.37). Across a whole rating, under 2 Kessler-10 points (editors' arithmetic).

claims.statement: In people who use classic psychedelics, feeling safe and supported is associated with fewer reported difficulties in retrospective surveys, while the one prospective study found only a weak, uncertain link for the place and the people. In that study (Haijen et al., 2018; about 198 self-selected adults planning their own experience), a good feeling about the people who would be present and about the place, rated within the day before, went with slightly lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores rated about a day after (standardized beta −0.14, p = 0.070, not statistically significant), and a retreat or a setting designed for therapy, reported afterwards as one yes-or-no item, was associated with no acute measure (0.02); the authors note that the term was not defined for participants. In an international online survey of 6,877 self-selected people who had drunk ayahuasca, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety at their last ceremony went with 0.29 points less extreme fear or panic on a 0-to-10 scale (95% CI 0.15 to 0.43, editors' calculation), slightly fewer difficulties in the weeks after, and current distress lower by 0.62 points on the 40-point Kessler scale, under 2 points across the whole rating (editors' arithmetic), after adjustment for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink; the ratings were made looking back by the same people, and averaged near the top of the scale (Perkins et al., 2021). Among 613 US adults in an online panel who had used a classic psychedelic, those who blamed a lack of psychological support for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.25) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (adjusted odds ratio 2.85, 95% CI 1.27 to 6.42; 41 of the 613 reported any); blaming a disagreeable physical environment went with a smaller difference in challenge (0.09) and none in harm thoughts, and blaming the people around with neither (odds ratio for harm thoughts 0.33, 0.11 to 1.01) (Simonsson et al., 2023). Among 163 experienced people recalling two experiences, mostly at home or at a friend's house, those whose experience was at a party, club or festival (24 first and 12 most recent experiences) had higher average challenge scores than the rest (19 against 17 and 31 against 16 per cent of the maximum), a comparison the authors did not test (Palmer and Maynard, 2022). No study compared settings by design. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
